title: Design: Time-Based Key-Value Store
oneLiner: A key-value store that remembers every version: get(key, t) returns the value set at the latest time at or before t. Each key keeps its versions in time order, so a binary search finds the answer.
keyTakeaway: Map each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs. Timestamps for a key arrive in increasing order, so appending keeps the list sorted for free. get(key, t) is then "the last timestamp <= t", an upper-bound binary search: O(log m) for m versions of that key, and O(1) for set.
explanation:
Design a class TimeMap with Set(key, value, timestamp), which stores value for key at that time, and Get(key, timestamp), which returns the value whose set time is the largest one at or before timestamp, or "" if there is none. For one key, set calls arrive with strictly increasing timestamps. Set foo = bar at 1, then Get(foo, 3) is bar; after Set foo = bar2 at 4, Get(foo, 4) and Get(foo, 5) are bar2, while Get(foo, 3) would still be bar.

The grader runs a list of operations and collects what every get returns. Arguments arrive as strings, so the harness converts the timestamps to integers for you.

Store a dictionary from key to a list of (timestamp, value). Set appends to that key's list. Because timestamps only increase, each list is already sorted by time, with no sorting needed.

Get searches the key's list for the last entry with timestamp <= t. Scanning backwards works but is O(m) per call. Binary search makes it O(log m): find the first entry with timestamp > t (lo = 0, hi = count; while lo < hi: mid; if times[mid] <= t then lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid), and the answer is the entry just before it, lo - 1. If lo is 0, every version is newer than t: return "". A missing key also returns "".

Set is O(1) amortized and Get is O(log m). This is the shape of multi-version storage: databases keep row versions with timestamps so each transaction reads the version that was current when it started (MVCC, in the Databases section), and configuration and feature-flag systems answer "what was the value at time t" the same way.

The visualization stores four versions of one key and answers Get at time 25.

visualizationSteps.message: Four Set calls for one key, at times 10, 20, 30 and 40. Appending kept them in time order. Now Get(key, 25).
Search slots 0 to 3: time 30 is > 25, so look earlier: hi = 2.
Search slots 0 to 1: time 20 is <= 25, so the answer is here or later: lo = 2.
lo = 2: the first version after 25. The one before it, slot 1, was current at 25: "low".

recognitionSignals: "Value as of time t", versioned data, snapshots: a sorted list per key plus binary search.
Data arrives already sorted by the field you will search on: append and binary search instead of a tree.
gotchas: Returning the first timestamp >= t instead of the last one <= t.
A query earlier than every version must return "", not the earliest value.
Off by one in the search: with an upper-bound search, the answer is at lo - 1.
confusableWith: Binary Search Range (first and last position) uses the same lower and upper bound searches on one array; here there is one sorted array per key.
LRU Cache also wraps a dictionary in extra structure, but evicts old entries; this keeps every version.

complexity.note: Set appends in O(1) amortized. Get binary-searches one key's versions, O(log m) for m versions of that key, which is at most O(log n). Every stored version is kept: O(n) for n set calls.
